catalog_quote: In this section, I provide an overview of the tone system in Bago by defining its distribution, realization and function in nouns and verbs. There are only two tonal rules in the language which are observed in finite verb formation and suffixation of number affixes. The language contrasts two levels of tone: high and low. In the transcription, a high tone is marked by an acute accent, and a low tone is unmarked. Lexically, tone plays an important role in determining the meaning of a word. The following pairs differ in their meanings solely as a result of their tonal patterns. [p. 47] ... In addition to the two levels, a contour tone is formed only in a heavy syllable. A falling or a raising contour is never found on a short vowel. A nasal segment is a tone-bearing unit, as in many Niger-Congo languages (see Morrison, 2009 for Kibena; Dorvlo, 2008 for Logba). new_statements.rule_in_words: Bago is a two-tone (H/L) register-tone language with lexically contrastive tone, contour tones restricted to bimoraic syllables and the mora as tone-bearing unit. The source makes no statement about word stress at all (the words 'stress', 'stressed', 'prominence' do not occur in the 399-page thesis); no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: only two tonal rules (finite-verb formation, number-suffixation); HL pattern absent from infinitives; long vowels in verbs always carry a single level tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone description (nouns, verbs, suffixes); citation-form elicitation from one main Kusuntu-born consultant speaking Bago plus recorded texts. Describes the Bago variety, not Kusuntu.
new_statements.identity_note: Alansary 2021 describes the Bago variety (main consultant a native Kusuntu speaker fluent in Bago); Ethnologue/Glottolog treat Bago and Kusuntu as dialects of bago1245 [bqg], while Kleinewillinghöfer 2000, Moussa 2011 and Takougnandi 2016 treat them as closely related distinct languages (Alansary 2021: 6). The tone statement applies to Bago; nothing was opened for Kusuntu.

sources.note: Nothing: 'stress/stressed/prominence' never occur (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing). Ch. 2 (pp. 17-56) gives consonants, vowels, vowel length/harmony, syllable structure and a tone section 2.4 (pp. 47-56): two level tones H and L, lexically contrastive; contour tones only on heavy syllables (long vowels, nasal codas); mora = tone-bearing unit; tone rules in finite-verb formation and number suffixation. Describes the Bago variety (consultant a Kusuntu native who speaks Bago); author treats Bago and Kusuntu as closely related but distinct (p. 6).
